Banger paper from Anthropic, Harvard, and colleagues.

They find that LLM-proposed quantum circuits beat the best-known designs on seven of eight tasks, with fewer Toffoli gates and fewer qubits.

They search over these circuit-generating programs with OpenEvolve, using Claude Mythos 5 to propose architectures and program rewrites.

LLMs propose circuit designs, an independent evaluator verifies correctness and scores the cost, and the best designs seed the next round.

The tasks cover numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory.

fullText:
The biggest gap between AI labs isn't whether their agents get the job done. It's whether users actually enjoy working with them.

We tracked the best agent from @AnthropicAI, @OpenAI, @GoogleDeepMind, @Kimi_Moonshot, @SpaceXSI and @deepseek_ai across 4 key Agent Arena signals used between late June and the start of October to see how the industry is shifting.

Three things stood out:
1. Users like some agents far more than others.

On Praise vs Complaint, OpenAI and Anthropic sit at +35 points over the leaderboard average. Moonshot, xAI and DeepSeek land between +5 and +13. No other signal splits the labs this widely.

2. Agents are getting much better at delivery.

On Confirmed Success, the average lab's best model went from -4 to +14 points in three months. Anthropic leads with Claude Opus 5.5 (Max) at +20.

3. Labs are converging on error recovery and steering.

Since June, the spread between the six labs has more than halved on Bash Recovery (34 → 16 points) and nearly halved on Steerability (19 → 11).

In short, the labs are catching up on avoiding failures.

Leaving the user happy is where the top three are pulling away.

fullText:
In 2022, Berkeley PhD student Woosuk Kwon thought he could make Meta's new open-weight model, OPT-175B, run faster in two weeks.

Four years and 3,000 contributors later, that project is @vllm_project, one of the largest open-source inference engines, running on ~500,000 GPUs at any given time.

He and fellow researchers Simon Mo, Kaichao You, and Roger Wang borrowed "virtual memory" from operating systems, handing out memory only as it's needed so each GPU can juggle requests of wildly different sizes. (The "v" in vLLM is for virtual.)

Their first user, Berkeley neighbor @arena, cut its GPU needs in half. Today Google, Amazon, and Meta all run vLLM in production.

In January, the core maintainers founded @inferact and raised $150M to give vLLM a full-time team.

They're hiring across eng, marketing, and devrel in SF and Singapore: https://t.co/DpODvfJWtC

// FDE-Gym: Agents as Forward-Deployed Engineers //

They found that the best agent configuration fully resolved 14 of 95 real customer-delivery tasks.

FDE-Gym tests agents as forward-deployed engineers. Each task comes from a real delivery project. Agents must question scripted stakeholders, work in production-like systems, and find constraints the customer never stated.

A delivery is scored by how much it improves the customer's own success metric, with penalties for extra messages, trial runs, and waiting time.

Across 13 configurations from seven providers, the top mean score is 0.56. The main failure is missing unstated constraints. Even on 23 tasks where the best configuration collected every key fact, it reached 0.8 or higher on only 10.

Highly recommended benchmark to look at.

fullText:
Banger paper from Google DeepMind on long-horizon multi-agent coding.

(bookmark it)

They report that, to the best of their knowledge, this is the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents.

They report that four Gemini 4 Argon agents beat Minecraft end-to-end. They defeated the Ender Dragon in 27 hours and 14 minutes with no human intervention.

Each agent controlled one player through the standard Mineflayer library. No one assigned roles, wrote game logic, or scouted a seed in advance. The agents planned, wrote, and debugged every program themselves, and coordinated through in-game chat and a shared memory.

Over the run, they wrote 2,783 programs and died 605 times. They split the work, shared what they learned, and recovered each other's items after deaths.

If you build agents for long software or enterprise tasks, this is a useful case study. The team had to keep one plan consistent across thousands of dependent steps for more than a day.

有点ChatGPT的Intelligent UI“进阶反面”的意思，Agentic App应该是一款AI可直接参与操作、用户也能通过可视化界面实时参与和接管的软件

在交互层面，人可以用图形界面，也可以用自然语言向Agent表达目标；Agent直接调用业务Action执行，两种方式可以结合

架构层面，通过Shared Actions、Shared Data、Shared Application State让两者操作的是同一套应用能力和状态，权限与验证也随之统一

Human+Agent原生协作是一个值得关注的方向，如果可行，未来软件无需再把所有操作都设计成一连串按钮、菜单、表单，用户可以直接表达目标让Agent操作，必要时再通过可视化界面介入

My summary:

💎 Don’t just plug your data into some formula to find the answers to the questions you started with. Real Data Science seeks and discovers the hidden questions in your data that you should be asking. Find the questions first, then seek their answers. 

💎 Don’t just use your data. Allow your data to use you — to challenge your assumptions, to twist your thinking, to slap you into seeing the greater realities that the data represents, to shock and surprise you, and to take you down rabbit holes into a data wonderland you never imagined. Your data should point the way and guide you, not vice versa. 

💎 One number is not a pattern. Find the meaningful patterns in the complex fabric of your data. Be sure you know (and be prepared to change) what you consider to be “meaningful”. Challenge your assumptions and your definitions as the deeper patterns in your data unfold.

💎  Look at your data. Master the art and science of data profiling — having your first date with your data. Remember Anscombe’s quartet and the Datasaurus Dozen: https://t.co/z0mS1dknYJ

Shakespeare said “All the world’s a stage”, though he could just as well said “graph” there, since both graphs and stage plays are all about entities and their relationships. And so is the world!

💎  Outliers are not annoyances to dismiss.  Three-sigma clipping might be throwing away your most significant,  meaningful, valuable, brilliant discovery. Been there. Done that. Never again!

fullText:
Fascinating paper from Google DeepMind.

They studied a market where AI agents bid to answer each user prompt.

Each agent bids its expected reward minus its inference cost. A first-price auction is simple to run, but bidders shade their bids, so a prompt can go to an agent that would not have produced the most value.

The paper shows two features of agent markets that keep this loss small. When several agents value a prompt close to the best one, for example because strong models are distilled into cheaper ones, competition limits the loss. When values mostly depend on how hard the prompt is, efficiency approaches 1 - 1/e^2 of optimal, well above the general bound of 1 - 1/e.

They find that simulations on the EmbedLLM routing dataset match the theory.

https://t.co/7cLDnMozvy
